content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published a pocket guide titled Clinical Management of Patients with Viral Haemorrhagic Fever: A Pocket Guide for Front-line Health Workers. This guide serves as interim emergency guidance for country adaptation and focuses on the clinical management of viral haemorrhagic fevers (VHFs), particularly in resource-limited settings. It was first published in March 2014 and updated in February 2016 to reflect lessons learned during the West African Ebola epidemic. Viral haemorrhagic fever (VHF) is a term used to describe severe illnesses caused by a variety of viruses, some of which are associated with bleeding. These viruses belong to families such as Arenaviridae (e.g., Lassa, Lujo), Bunyaviridae (e.g., Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever [CCHF]), Filoviridae (e.g., Ebola, Marburg), and Flaviviridae (e.g., yellow fever, dengue). This guide focuses on VHFs that occur in Africa and have the potential for person-to-person transmission, such as Ebola, Marburg, CCHF, Lassa fever, and Lujo. It does not address other viral infections like dengue or yellow fever, which may have haemorrhagic manifestations but are not transmitted directly between individuals. The guide aims to provide clear, evidence-based recommendations for the clinical management of VHFs, including infection prevention and control (IPC) measures. It is designed to support front-line health workers in triage, case definition, early and ongoing case management, and safe hospital discharge. The recommendations are drawn from published VHF guidelines, WHO normative guidance, and clinical algorithms for diarrhoeal diseases, sepsis, and other conditions. The 2014–2015 Ebola epidemic in West Africa highlighted the need for effective case management and infection control. The large number of cases required the establishment of new Ebola Treatment Units (ETUs) and holding centres, as well as extensive training and mentoring of health workers. Lessons learned during this epidemic emphasized the importance of supportive care, particularly fluid resuscitation and the correction of electrolyte imbalances, in reducing case fatality rates. Inadequate fluid resuscitation was identified as a common issue in many ETUs, underscoring the need for improved clinical practices. The guide also addresses the management of other VHFs, such as Lassa fever, which is endemic in West Africa and requires differentiation from Ebola through laboratory testing. Ribavirin is effective for Lassa fever and CCHF but not for Ebola or Marburg, highlighting the importance of accurate diagnosis. The guide provides practical approaches to fluid administration using oral rehydration solutions (ORS), intravenous (IV), and intraosseous (IO) fluids, even in challenging conditions where personal protective equipment (PPE) limits the time and dexterity of health workers. In addition to clinical management, the guide includes guidance on IPC measures to minimize nosocomial transmission and improve early recognition of VHFs. It emphasizes the importance of maintaining a high level of suspicion for VHFs, particularly in the early stages of an outbreak when symptoms may resemble other common infections like malaria or typhoid. Separate notes are provided for the care of children and pregnant women. The guide does not cover the creation of VHF treatment units or community interventions to control transmission but is intended to complement such efforts. It aims to strengthen the overall response to VHF outbreaks in Africa and contribute to compliance with international health regulations. By providing systematic approaches to VHF management, the guide seeks to build the capacity and confidence of health workers to safely and effectively manage these life-threatening diseases.
